problem: Two exponents are missing their superscripts, so the formulas read wrongly. |H(jω)|² = 1/(1 + (ω/ωc)2n) reads as (ω/ωc)×2n instead of (ω/ωc) raised to 2n, and ε = √(10Ap/10 − 1) reads as √(Ap − 1) instead of √(10^(Ap/10) − 1). A student will substitute the wrong value.
fix: Write |H(jω)|² = 1/(1 + (ω/ωc)<sup>2n</sup>) and ε = √(10<sup>Ap/10</sup> − 1). Say in words that Ap/10 is the exponent of 10.

problem: The order formula is printed as n ≥ log10(10As/10 − 1)/(2 log10(fs/fc)) and the quiz as log10(1040/10 − 1). Taken literally these are 10×As/10 = As and 1040/10 = 104, so both computations come out wrong even though the numeric answers (n = 7) assume the correct expression.
fix: Write n ≥ log10(10<sup>As/10</sup> − 1)/(2 log10(fs/fc)) in Section 3 and log10(10<sup>40/10</sup> − 1) in Quiz Q8.

problem: 'Frequency scaling multiplies every resistor by m and divides every capacitor by m; fc and Q stay the same' is not frequency scaling: multiplying R by m and dividing C by m leaves RC and hence fc unchanged; that is impedance scaling. Labelling it frequency scaling, and then repeating it as 'impedance scaling does the same', leaves the student with no working rule for moving fc.
fix: State two separate rules. Frequency scaling to a new cut-off fc′: divide every capacitor by k or divide every resistor by k, where k = fc′/fc; fc becomes fc′ and Q is unchanged. Impedance scaling: multiply every resistor by m and divide every capacitor by m; fc and Q stay the same and the impedance level rises by m.

where: Section 2 (last sentence of the scaling block)
problem: The resistor rule is inverted: 'to move from fc to fc′, scale all capacitors by fc/fc′ or all resistors by fc′/fc'. Raising the cut-off requires smaller resistors, so multiplying R by fc′/fc lowers fc instead of raising it; the capacitor and resistor rules must use the same factor.
fix: To move a designed filter from fc to fc′, scale all capacitors by fc/fc′ or scale all resistors by fc/fc′ (equivalently, divide the resistors by fc′/fc).

where: Worked example 1, step 1 and Quiz Q3
problem: The powers of ten are printed without superscripts: 'C = 10 × 10−9 F', '1/(2π × 104 × 10−8)'. As typed these read as 10 × 10 − 9 and 104 × 10 − 8 and the arithmetic cannot be checked.
fix: Write C = 10 × 10<sup>−9</sup> F in step 1 and 1/(2π × 10<sup>4</sup> × 10<sup>−8</sup>) in Quiz Q3.

problem: The same name is used for two different numbers: earlier 'damping factor ζ = 1/√2' (0.707) and later 'd = 1/Q the damping factor; d = 1.414'. A student will think the text contradicts itself.
fix: Keep ζ as the damping ratio with Q = 1/(2ζ), and call d = 1/Q = 2ζ the dissipation factor (some syllabi say damping), noting that d = 1.414 for a Butterworth section, i.e. twice ζ.

problem: 'A 5% error in R shifts fc by about 5% and also changes Q' is misleading. In the equal-component Sallen-Key, Q = 1/(3 − K) is set only by K = 1 + Rf/R1; an equal shift in both filter resistors changes fc and leaves Q unchanged. Only mismatch between the two resistors or capacitors, or tolerance in Rf and R1, moves Q.
fix: Say: a 5% error in R shifts fc by about 5%; Q is set by the gain K = 1 + Rf/R1, so it is mismatch between the two filter resistors or capacitors, and the tolerance of Rf and R1, that changes Q. High-Q sections are the sensitive ones.

problem: The example rounds R to 8.2 kΩ but never states that the cut-off then moves away from the specified 2 kHz, so a student may believe the final circuit still cuts off at exactly 2 kHz.
fix: Add: with R = 8.2 kΩ and C = 10 nF the actual cut-off is 1/(2π × 8.2 kΩ × 10 nF) ≈ 1.94 kHz, about 3% low; use 7.96 kΩ (or trim R) if the 2 kHz value matters.
